$comment: What a release of mcpp-language-server carries. This file is the declaration; `mcppls-devtools release check` (modules/pack/src/release.cpp) checks a staged release directory against it and refuses a release that is missing a required asset or carrying one nobody declared. Prose describing a release goes stale silently; this does not.

assets.what: The VS Code extension, one for every system: it carries the one payload, whose entry for the machine it runs on starts the server
assets.install: `code --install-extension <file>`, or the Extensions view's “Install from VSIX…”

assets.what: The server, the clangd of every platform and the openkal semantic kit, as one tree (`payload/`). The server is the one okb of every architecture (`bin/mcppls.okb`); payload.json's entry for each platform names the runner that starts it (`libexec/okrun/<system>-<arch>/okrun[.exe]`) and the clangd it drives (`clangd/<platform>/`). The VSIX and the CLion plugin carry these bytes; Zed and Neovim use it installed beside their plugin
assets.install: Unpack it; `payload/libexec/okrun/<system>-<arch>/okrun payload/bin/mcppls.okb serve` speaks LSP over stdio. For a command named `mcppls`, use the openkal package or a single file below

assets.what: The Zed extension directory `mcppls-zed/`: extension.toml, the compiled extension.wasm and the crate it was compiled from, which Zed's dev-extension install compiles again. Platform-independent; the server comes from PATH or the installed payload
assets.install: Unpack it, then Zed's command palette: `zed: install dev extension`, and choose `mcppls-zed` (Zed compiles it, which needs Rust through rustup). The server is `mcppls` on PATH (the openkal package or a single file), else the payload `mcppls-devtools extension --editor zed --install` puts in place

assets.what: The CLion plugin, one for every system, with the one payload inside it (`mcppls-clion/payload/`), so it needs nothing else installed. Gradle and the JDK it compiles with come from the `clion` feature (xim:gradle)
assets.install: The JetBrains Marketplace, or CLion: Settings → Plugins → the gear menu → *Install Plugin from Disk*, and restart

assets.what: The server for every system and architecture as one package (mcpp's tree of the `openkal` set): both architectures' images under `lib/<arch>/`, the launchers `bin/mcppls` (POSIX) and `bin/mcppls.exe` (Windows), and the platform's runner of Linux x86_64 and aarch64, macOS arm64 and Windows x86_64 under `libexec/okrun/`, so it needs nothing installed; its mcpp-package.json says where it runs (`runs_on`). The server alone: clangd and the kits come from a payload, PATH or xlings
assets.install: Unpack it and put its `bin/` on PATH; `mcppls serve` speaks LSP over stdio

assets.what: The server as one okb (openkal's image package): the image of x86_64 and of aarch64, which the platform's runner of any system starts. The payload, and so every editor's plugin, carries these bytes as `bin/mcppls.okb`
assets.install: `okrun mcppls-{version}.okb serve`, with the platform's runner of this system: the payload's or the openkal package's `libexec/okrun/<system>-<arch>/okrun`

assets.what: The server as one executable file for Linux x86_64: the platform's carrier with the image inside, which it runs from memory; nothing to unpack or install (a static program)
assets.install: Rename it `mcppls`, put it on PATH and `chmod +x` it; `mcppls serve` speaks LSP over stdio

assets.what: The server as one executable file for Linux aarch64: the platform's carrier with the image inside, which it runs from memory; nothing to unpack or install (a static program)
assets.install: Rename it `mcppls`, put it on PATH and `chmod +x` it; `mcppls serve` speaks LSP over stdio

assets.what: The server as one executable file for macOS arm64: the platform's carrier with the image inside, which it runs from memory; nothing to unpack or install
assets.install: Rename it `mcppls`, put it on PATH and `chmod +x` it; `mcppls serve` speaks LSP over stdio

assets.what: The server as one executable file for Windows x86_64: the platform's carrier with the image inside, which it runs from memory; nothing to unpack or install
assets.install: Rename it `mcppls.exe`, put it on PATH; `mcppls serve` speaks LSP over stdio

assets.what: The openkal semantic kit (spec S4, kit-version 2), the one the payload carries: libc++ headers and the `std` and `std.compat` module sources, openkal-musl's headers, and the generated headers of each architecture. With it a project is read without a compiler for any target: `import std` and the standard library work, a system's own headers and macros do not. Its version is the openkal platform's
assets.install: `xlings install mcppls-kit-openkal`, or unpack it into the xlings store as `xim-x-mcppls-kit-openkal/<version>/`

assets.what: The semantic kit of one target (spec S4): libc++ headers and module sources of the clangd's LLVM release, and the system's C library headers where they may be shipped (macOS: the installed SDK). The server installs the kit of a project's target with xlings once the editor asks; this file is the same kit for a machine without the network
assets.install: `xlings install mcppls-kit-<target>@<version>`, or unpack it into the xlings store as `xim-x-mcppls-kit-<target>/<version>/`

assets.what: sha256 of every other file in the release
This declaration, rendered for the release page: every file, what it is, and how to install it

not-in-a-release: The Claude Code plugin: it is consumed from the repository through its marketplace file, not downloaded as an archive.
The rendered xim-pkgindex descriptors (`mcppls-devtools release xlings`): they name these assets by their URLs and go to xim-pkgindex, not to the release page.
The model gateway: a separate package, built and tested on its own, not part of what a user installs.
